analysis.one_liner: Sets a national goal to cut child poverty in half and requires annual government reporting on progress.
analysis.headline: The bill set a goal of halving child poverty in five years and required annual public tracking of it, but died in the Senate Finance Committee without a hearing, a markup, or a vote.
analysis.plain_summary: The Child Poverty Reduction Act would make it official policy of the United States to cut the number of children living in poverty in half within five years. To hold the government to that goal, it requires the Census Bureau and the Department of Health and Human Services to publish an annual child poverty rate using a measure anchored to inflation, and requires the National Academy of Sciences to report each year on how well federal programs are working. It funds the studies with about $7.6 million in authorizations over a decade but changes no benefits itself.
analysis.who_benefits: The roughly 11 million American children counted as poor under the supplemental poverty measure would gain an official, annually updated, inflation-adjusted poverty rate, plus independent yearly analysis of which federal programs actually reduce child poverty. That gives advocates, journalists, and lawmakers a common yardstick and a public record of which policies work. The changes are measurement and accountability only; the bill creates no new benefits or payments to families.
analysis.who_benefits_short: Children in poverty, via better public tracking

how_it_helps.text: Declares it the policy of the United States to halve the number of children in poverty within five years, with a stated aim of also reducing deep poverty and poverty among racial and ethnic groups with the highest rates.

Requires an annually reported, inflation-anchored supplemental poverty measure for children, released alongside the Census Bureau's main income and poverty report, so child poverty is tracked on a fixed yardstick every year.

Requires the National Academy of Sciences to publish annual, nonpartisan analyses of how federal policies affect child poverty and to update the 2019 'Roadmap to Reduce Child Poverty' and study intergenerational poverty.
Requires the Census Bureau to correct income data for underreporting and to report child poverty for Puerto Rico, Guam, and other territories.

analysis.who_pays: Federal taxpayers, through roughly $7.6 million in authorized spending over ten years for Census data work and National Academy studies. No household, industry, or program loses benefits or revenue under the bill.

drawbacks.text: The bill changes no benefits and creates no programs. Its five-year goal is a 'statement of policy' and a 'sense of the Congress,' which are nonbinding, so a government could miss the goal entirely without any consequence.

An anchored poverty threshold fixed at one point in time and adjusted only for prices means the official yardstick would not reflect rising living standards, a design choice poverty researchers debate, and the bill explicitly does not replace the Census Bureau's existing measures.
The bill authorizes but does not guarantee appropriations, so its reporting and studies could go unfunded even if enacted.

analysis.benefit_vs_cost: The cost is trivial (millions per year for studies and data work) against a problem affecting millions of children, but the benefit is also indirect: this is a measurement and accountability bill, not an anti-poverty program. Its real value is forcing the government to publish, every year, whether child poverty is rising or falling and which policies are working. Someone who believes poverty needs money and programs rather than more reports would reasonably call it insufficient; it does not pretend to cut poverty on its own.

outcome.mechanism: It was introduced and sent to the Senate Finance Committee, which never took it up, so it expired when the Congress ended in January 2025.

narrative.text: Senator Casey introduced the bill with Senators Baldwin and Brown on September 21, 2023, and it was read twice and referred to the Committee on Finance.
The bill received two cosponsors, both Senate Democrats, and no further action was taken after the referral to Finance.
No hearing, markup, committee vote, or floor vote ever occurred before the 118th Congress ended on January 3, 2025.

outcome.who_came_out_ahead: No one gained anything concrete from the bill dying, since it would have changed only measurement and reporting. The status quo prevailed: child poverty continues to be tracked under the Census Bureau's existing measures, and no annual accountability reporting on halving child poverty was created.

analysis.who_came_out_ahead_short: No one; the status quo held

for.name: Sen. Robert Casey Jr.
for.what_they_did: Introduced the Child Poverty Reduction Act of 2023 in the Senate.

for.name: Sens. Tammy Baldwin and Sherrod Brown
for.role: Original cosponsors, U.S. Senators from Wisconsin and Ohio

against.name: Senate Finance Committee
against.role: Committee of referral, chaired by Sen. Ron Wyden (D-OR)
against.what_they_did: Received the bill on referral and took no further action — no hearing, markup, or vote — for the remaining sixteen months of the Congress.

sides.party_line_note: No vote was ever taken. The bill's three sponsors were all Democrats, and no Republican cosponsored it, but no senator spoke or voted against it either.

industries.industry: National Academy of Sciences and academic poverty researchers
industries.note: The bill would have funneled roughly $7.6 million in authorized funds into National Academies studies and annual child poverty analysis. Those studies would have informed public policy rather than commercial gain.
